newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-WALLABIES' FUTURE BRIGHT WITHOUT ME, SAYS CAMPO.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-WALLABIES' FUTURE BRIGHT WITHOUT ME, SAYS CAMPO.

text.p: David Campese is confident the next generation of Wallabies can loosen New Zealand's grip on world rugby in the lead-up to the 1999 World Cup even without his familiar presence in the number 11 jersey.

The lack of a test against England robbed a developing Australian team of the chance to secure a complete European 'grand slam' but few touring sides go home with a 100 percent record and test wins over Italy, Scotland, Ireland and Wales.

"The team proved they've got the potential to be a great team...to go home undefeated is another great Wallaby achievement," insisted Campese, having contributed one farewell try in Australia's 39-12 victory over the Barbarians on Saturday.

Barring an offer even he cannot refuse, the 34-year-old winger seems likely to reject approaches to play club rugby in England and return home to play one more season with New South Wales in the Super 12 tournament.
He leaves behind a team still in transition and lacking the individual stars of recent years but coach Greg Smith believes his persistent detractors are being unfair.

"We are happy because we've accomplished a lot. Contrary to what some journalists think, the opposition we've played against has not been substandard. We've been given teams to play, we've played them and we've beaten them. You can't do more than that.

"There are certain areas of the team where we need to develop but as most of the results in the Tri-Nations series indicated we're not that far away from South Africa and New Zealand. New Zealand are the best team in the world, the team you've got to chase, but I think there's a lot of encouragement for Australia. We've now got a fairly broad base to pick from."
Former Wallaby captain Nick Farr-Jones is among those not totally convinced and he felt a test against England would have answered a number of key questions.
"They haven't set the world on fire, with the exception perhaps of the Munster match," he said. "But they are undefeated and they've had some horrific injury problems so they can go home very proud.
"We didn't really find out how good they are but we're a few years away from a World Cup and I think we've got great talent."
The only Australian to make a current southern hemisphere dream team selected by Bob Dwyer is injured Wallaby captain John Eales but it will take a long time for images of Campese to fade.

He cited the opportunity "to play at Twickenham and Cardiff Arms Park and to pull on the Wallaby jersey" as his fondest memories and signed off in typical style by suggesting the Barbarians' backs had failed to fire because they contained too many British players.
"The Barbarians love to try and run the ball but I've noticed when there's a lot of British players in their side they're not used to it. Too often they go back into their shells."
Campese also continues to insist he has been misunderstood at home and abroad over the years.

"They know me as a footballer, they don't know me as a person. A lot of things I say to the press are what they want to hear, it's not what I think. What I said about England in 1991 might not have been the truth but it got them upset, didn't it? I'm not a stupid person. It's good tactics."
"Rugby needs characters...when (John) McEnroe and (Jimmy) Connors left tennis they said 'Thank God they've gone' but now they want them back."
